name: JUDGE-BENCH
description: An extensible collection of 20 NLP evaluation datasets with human annotations for benchmarking 11 LLMs' ability to replicate human judgment as evaluators. Tests whether LLMs can serve as reliable judges across diverse properties: grammaticality, factuality, instruction-following, creativity, coherence, and more. Finds that LLMs align well with humans on basic properties but show substantial variance on expert-annotated complex tasks.
evaluation_method: agreement with human annotations (Cohen's kappa, Spearman correlation)
general_score_metric: human-LLM agreement rate (correlation with human annotations)
typical_sota_score: High agreement (~0.7–0.9 correlation) on basic properties; drops significantly on expert-annotated complex properties
reputation: Published at ACL 2025; meta-evaluation of LLM-as-judge systems; critical for validating the increasingly popular LLM judge paradigm; 20 datasets covering diverse evaluation properties
notes: ACL 2025. Addresses the critical question of whether LLM-as-judge systems (widely used in benchmarks like MT-Bench, Arena-Hard, AlpacaEval) are actually reliable. Key finding: models tend to be more reliable when judging model-generated text than human-generated text, revealing 'homophily bias'. Simple properties (grammaticality, toxicity) show high agreement; complex properties (originality, scientific validity) show low agreement. 11 LLMs evaluated as judges across 20 NLP tasks.
